title: Gazelle
wiki_lead:
A gazelle is one of many antelope species in the genus Gazella . There are also seven species included in two further genera; Eudorcas and Nanger, which were formerly considered subgenera of Gazella. A third former subgenus, Procapra, includes three living species of Asian gazelles.
Gazelles are known as swift animals. Some can run at bursts as high as 100 km/h (60 mph) or run at a sustained speed of 50 km/h (30 mph). Gazelles are found mostly in the deserts, grasslands, and savannas of Africa, but they are also found in southwest and central Asia and the Indian subcontinent. They tend to live in herds, and eat fine, easily digestible plants and leaves.
Gazelles are relatively small antelopes, most standing 60–110 cm (2–3.5 ft) high at the shoulder, and are generally fawn-colored.
The gazelle genera are Gazella, Eudorcas, and Nanger. The taxonomy of these genera is confused, and the classification of species and subspecies has been an unsettled issue. Currently, the genus Gazella is widely considered to contain about 10 species. One species is extinct: the Queen of Sheba's gazelle. Most surviving gazelle species are considered threatened to varying degrees. Closely related to the true gazelles are the Tibetan goa, and Mongolian gazelles (species of the genus Procapra), the blackbuck of Asia, and the African springbok.
One widely familiar gazelle is the African species Thomson's gazelle (Eudorcas thomsonii), sometimes referred to as a "tommie". It is around 60 to 70 cm (24 to 28 in) in shoulder height and is coloured brown and white with a distinguishing black stripe. The males have long, often curved, horns. Like many other prey species, tommies exhibit a distinctive behaviour of stotting (running and jumping high before fleeing) when they are threatened by predators such as cheetahs, lions, African wild dogs, crocodiles, hyenas, and leopards.

Etymology

Gazelle is derived from French gazelle, Old French gazel, probably via Old Spanish gacel, probably from North African pronunciation of Arabic: غزال ġazāl, Maghrebi pronunciation ġazēl. To Europe it first came to Old Spanish and Old French, and then around 1600 the word entered the English language. The Arab people traditionally hunted the gazelle. Later appreciated for its grace, however, it became a symbol most commonly associated in Arabic literature with human beauty.


Species

The gazelles are divided into three genera and numerous species.


Prehistoric species
Fossils of genus Gazella are found in Miocene, Pliocene and Pleistocene deposits of Eurasia and Africa, which occupied a broader distribution that modern members of the genus. The earliest members of the genus are known from the Middle Miocene of Africa, around 14 million years ago with members of the genus inhabiting Europe from the Late Miocene until their extinction in the region during the Early Pleistocene around 1.8 million years ago.

In culture


Symbolism
The gazelle, like the antelope to which it is related, is the totem of many African families. Some examples include the Joof family of the Senegambia region, the Bagananoa of Botswana in Southern Africa (said to be descended from the BaHurutshe), and the Eraraka (or Erarak) clan of Uganda. As is common in many African societies, it is forbidden for the Joof or Eraraka to kill or touch the family totem.


Poetry
One of the traditional themes of Arabic love poetry involves comparing the gazelle with the beloved, and linguists theorize ghazal, the word for love poetry in Arabic, is related to the word for gazelle. The Caliph Abd al-Malik (646–705) freed a gazelle that he had captured because of her resemblance to his beloved:

The theme is found in the ancient Hebrew Song of Songs. (8:14)

grok_lead: A gazelle is a small to medium-sized antelope belonging to the family Bovidae, primarily within the genus Gazella and related genera such as Nanger and Eudorcas, characterized by its slender build, long legs, and exceptional speed for evading predators. Native to Africa and Asia, gazelles inhabit diverse arid and semi-arid environments including steppes, savannas, deserts, and semi-deserts, where they have adapted to survive with minimal water by extracting moisture from vegetation and digging for succulent plants. There are approximately 18 recognized species of gazelles, many of which exhibit sexual dimorphism with males featuring longer, lyre-shaped horns, and several are classified as vulnerable or endangered on the IUCN Red List due to habitat fragmentation, poaching, and competition with livestock. Gazelles are primarily herbivores that graze on grasses, herbs, and shrubs, often forming mixed diets that vary by species and season, with some like the goitered gazelle ( Gazella subgutturosa) consuming coastal seaweeds in certain regions. They are highly social animals, typically living in herds ranging from a few individuals to hundreds, which enhances predator detection and provides safety in numbers, though group composition shifts seasonally with males often forming bachelor herds outside breeding periods. A notable behavioral adaptation is stotting (or pronking), a stiff-legged vertical leap performed during predator encounters, believed to signal the gazelle's health and deter pursuit by demonstrating escape capability. Reproduction in gazelles is polygynous, with males defending territories or harems during rutting seasons, leading to births of single calves after a gestation of 5â7 months; many species seek habitats with cover for calving to reduce predation risk. Conservation efforts focus on protected areas, reintroduction programs, and anti-poaching measures, as species like the dama gazelle ( Nanger dama), the largest at up to 75 kg, have seen populations decline to fewer than 500 individuals in the wild as of 2024.
